name: Reference adult body mass
notes: THE ROW HANDOVER SECTION 9 SAYS IS MISSING: 'body_mass is not a ledger row and is the largest un-modelled dimorphism'. It was a hard-coded 70.0 default on three function signatures. It is now one number in one place and the model scales to it. ASSUMED, NOT SOURCED, AND DELIBERATELY SO. 70 kg is the conventional reference adult and it is entered here as the value the code already used, so that promoting it to the ledger changes NOTHING - size_factor returns exactly 1.0 and every existing result is bit-identical. Dressing it in a citation at the same time as changing the model structure would have made two changes at once and left neither testable. THE SEXED PAIR IS THE NEXT STEP AND THE SOURCE IS ALREADY WHITELISTED. SOURCES.md admits ICRP Publication 89 (reference anatomical and physiological values) as tier A, and it carries reference adult masses by sex. That extraction is NOT done here and the numbers are NOT guessed at: per directive 1.5 a citation nobody opened is worse than an honest assumption. When it lands this row becomes a male/female pair under ADR 0014 and, because every extensive quantity in the model now scales through it, it will move the whole model for both sexes at once - which is exactly what the handover means by calling body mass the largest un-modelled dimorphism. WHAT SCALES THROUGH IT: see src/scaling.jl. Extensive quantities scale linearly, intensive ones do not. Linear-in-mass is exact for the volumes, which are already entered as mass fractions, and is an APPROXIMATION for GFR and cardiac output, which are conventionally normalised to body surface area and therefore grow sub-linearly with mass. Linear scaling OVERSTATES their population spread. Fixing that needs height, which this model does not carry. Recorded as debt rather than approximated with an unsourced allometric exponent. CLARIFIED 2026-08-27 WHEN THE NHANES EXTRACTION LANDED. This row is the mass at which this ledger's EXTENSIVE CONSTANTS ARE STATED - GFR 180 L/day, CO 7200 mL/min, blood volume 5.0 L are textbook values for a roughly 70 kg, 1.73 m2 adult - so it is a normalisation convention belonging to those sources, NOT a claim about how much people weigh. It stays `both` and stays 70.0. The claim about people is BF.BODY_MASS.TYPICAL, which IS a male/female pair (90.3 / 77.9 kg, NHANES 2021-2023). Moving THIS row to a population mean would rescale every extensive constant against a denominator its own sources never used, turning GFR into 232 L/day by arithmetic rather than by measurement. The two rows are different quantities and ADR 0014 applies to each separately.

name: Typical adult body mass, population mean
citation: Fryar CD, Gu Q, Afful J, Carroll MD, Ogden CL. Anthropometric Reference Data for Children and Adults: United States, August 2021-August 2023. Vital and Health Statistics Series 3, No. 50. Atlanta (GA): National Center for Health Statistics; 2025 Jun. doi:10.15620/cdc/174595. Table 3, weight in kilograms for adults age 20 and older, by sex. Read from the NCBI Bookshelf reproduction of Table 3.
notes: NHANES TABLE 3, ADULTS AGE 20 AND OLDER. Male mean 90.3 kg (SEM 0.9, n = 2,688); female mean 77.9 kg (SEM 0.8, n = 3,254). Sample sizes unweighted, estimates weighted to the US population. Pregnant females excluded. Pre-registered in validation/body_mass_prereg.md, committed at 3fd859b before the source was opened. pooling_rule = single-source, k = 1. THIS IS NOT THE SAME QUANTITY AS BF.BODY_MASS.REFERENCE AND MUST NOT BE MERGED WITH IT. The reference row is the mass at which this ledger's EXTENSIVE CONSTANTS are stated - GFR 180 L/day, cardiac output 7200 mL/min, blood volume 5.0 L are all textbook values for a roughly 70 kg, 1.73 m2 adult. It is a normalisation convention belonging to those sources, not a claim about how much people weigh. THIS row is a claim about how much people weigh. Setting the reference to 90.3 would scale GFR to 232 L/day by construction, which is not a measurement of anything - it would restate the same physiology against a different denominator and silently rescale every constant whose source assumed 70 kg. The prereg said the sexed pair 'must move the model'. It moves the POPULATION, which is where body mass actually lives; the single-individual default stays at the reference so that no existing result moves for a reason unrelated to this extraction. WHAT THIS EXPOSES, AND IT IS NOT SMALL: a typical US adult male at 90.3 kg is 1.29x the reference mass, and scaling.jl already records that linear-in-mass scaling OVERSTATES the spread of GFR and cardiac output, which are properly normalised to body surface area. Applying linear scaling out to 1.29x is using it at the edge of where it is defensible. The US adult population this describes has a mean BMI in the obese range, so the model's typical individual is now heavier than the lean reference adults in whom GFR0 and CO0 were characterised. That is a real limitation of using a population survey as a physiological reference and it is recorded rather than hidden.

name: Adult body mass, 5th percentile
citation: Fryar CD, Gu Q, Afful J, Carroll MD, Ogden CL. Anthropometric Reference Data for Children and Adults: United States, August 2021-August 2023. Vital and Health Statistics Series 3, No. 50. Atlanta (GA): National Center for Health Statistics; 2025 Jun. doi:10.15620/cdc/174595. Table 3, weight in kilograms for adults age 20 and older, by sex. Read from the NCBI Bookshelf reproduction of Table 3.
notes: NHANES Table 3 percentile, adults 20 and older, same source and extraction as BF.BODY_MASS.TYPICAL. Entered as a PERCENTILE, NOT converted to a standard deviation, and that is deliberate. The source reports a standard error of the MEAN and a percentile distribution; it does not report a population SD. Two standard estimators disagree materially because body weight is right-skewed - (P95-P05)/3.29 gives 21.6 kg for males while IQR/1.349 gives 18.7 kg, and the male mean 90.3 sits above the median 86.6 - so picking one AFTER seeing the numbers is exactly the unfalsifiable choice validation/pooling.md exists to prevent, and the pre-registration did not declare an SD estimator. NO SD IS ENTERED. The ensemble samples Sobol between these bounds, which is what sample_population actually does with its argument anyway - it only ever took the 1st and 99th percentiles of the distribution it was handed and sampled uniformly between them. KNOWN LIMITATION, now explicit rather than disguised by a Normal: the sampled population is UNIFORM over this range, not weight-distributed, so it over-represents the tails. Fixing that needs a declared distribution family and an SD estimator chosen in advance, which is its own pre-registration.

name: Relative amplitude of circadian modulation of renal sodium handling
citation: Kanabrocki EL, Scheving LE, Olwin JH, et al. Circadian variation in the urinary excretion of electrolytes and trace elements in men. Am J Anat 1983;166(2):121-148.
notes: STILL ASSUMED AT 0.25, AND NOW WITH THE CONFLICT RECORDED RATHER THAN A SINGLE SOURCE. A wide sweep of the circadian sodium literature found the amplitude genuinely contested. UPPER END: Kanabrocki 1983, 11 healthy adult males, 3-hourly urine over 27 h with cosinor analysis, found a statistically significant population rhythm for sodium and reported that for almost every element the increase from lowest to highest 3-hour group mean exceeded 100%. A peak-to-trough ratio of 2 corresponds to a cosinor amplitude of 0.33, and >100% is a lower bound, so this supports 0.33 or more. LOWER END: Peng 2021, 85 healthy Chinese adults, every voided specimen over 24 h with cosinor analysis, found URINARY SODIUM SHOWED NON-SIGNIFICANT PARAMETERS IN THE COSINOR MODEL and that the sodium rhythm was less significant than potassium. That is close to an amplitude of zero. 0.25 sits between them and is NOT a pooled estimate - pooling a significant and a non-significant result is not defensible. THE RHYTHM'S EXISTENCE IS BETTER SUPPORTED THAN ITS SIZE: see CIRC.RENAL_NA.ENDOGENEITY_MARKER. THE PROPER SOURCE HAS BEEN IDENTIFIED AND NOT YET OBTAINED - Minors and Waterhouse 1990 provide normative ENDOGENOUS urinary sodium data from about 80 constant routines, which is exactly the unmasked quantity this parameter should carry. Get it before trusting any circadian sodium result.

name: Time of peak renal sodium excretion
citation: Ueno M, Kawasaki T, Uezono K, Omae T, Matsuoka M. Relationship of urinary kallikrein excretion to renal water and sodium excretion. Metabolism 1983;32(5):433-437.
notes: STILL ASSUMED AT 0.33 day, AND THE ACROPHASE IS CONTESTED TOO - the two best cosinor studies found are nearly ANTIPHASE. Ueno 1983, 20 healthy Japanese women on an ordinary diet, cosinor: acrophase of urinary sodium excretion at 16:55, i.e. late afternoon, closely tracking urine volume at 16:51 (r = 0.935). Under this component's convention with a 07:00 active-period start that is 0.41 day. Peng 2021, 85 healthy Chinese adults, cosinor: sodium excretion had a NOCTURNAL PEAK falling to its lowest around noon to afternoon - roughly the opposite. 0.33 day (about 15:00) is retained as a placeholder consistent with Ueno and inconsistent with Peng. It is NOT a compromise between them; there is no defensible compromise between antiphase estimates. Resolve with the Minors and Waterhouse constant-routine normative data before this parameter is used for anything.

name: Endogenous circadian amplitude of mean arterial pressure, relative
citation: Shea SA, Hilton MF, Hu K, Scheer FAJL. Existence of an endogenous circadian blood pressure rhythm in humans that peaks in the evening. Circ Res 2011;108(8):980-984.
notes: PRECISION: rounded to 2 significant figures on 2026-08-27. The sources do not support more, and carrying digits that do not exist forced the closure gate and the test suite to chase arithmetic noise. Derived rows inherit the significant figures of their inputs and are rounded to match; the closure tolerance was moved to 1e-3 in the same change, which is still an order of magnitude tighter than the 6% error that motivated that gate. || REPLACES CIRC.CV_MAP.DIP_FRACTION = 0.15, WHICH WAS THE WRONG QUANTITY BY ABOUT NINE TIMES AND ALSO THE WRONG PHASE. That parameter encoded the 10-20% NOCTURNAL AMBULATORY DIP as though it were the endogenous circadian driver. It is not. Degaute 1991 (31 healthy young men, ambulatory BP with simultaneous polysomnography) found RECUMBENCY AND SLEEP ACCOUNT FOR 65-75% OF THE NOCTURNAL DECLINE, concluding that posture and the wake-sleep transition are the major factors in the 24-h BP rhythm. THE ENDOGENOUS COMPONENT IS REAL BUT SMALL. Shea 2011 measured it under three complementary protocols in 28 normotensive adults - a 38-h constant routine and forced desynchrony at 28-h and 20-h sleep/wake cycles - and found significant circadian rhythms in all three with almost identical profiles: peak-to-trough 3-6 mmHg systolic and 2-3 diastolic. Converting through MAP = DBP + (SBP-DBP)/3 gives 2.33-4.00 mmHg peak-to-trough, so a cosinor amplitude of 0.0125 to 0.0215 of MAP. Midpoint adopted, range carried. DERIVED because the MAP conversion is arithmetic on reported SBP and DBP, not a reported MAP amplitude. LIVE CONTROVERSY, RECORDED NOT RESOLVED: Kerkhof 1998 (25 normotensives, 26-h constant routine, stated power >0.95) found NO significant endogenous BP rhythm, and Van Dongen 2001 replicated that absence five times in six subjects. Shea's forced-desynchrony design separates circadian from behavioural influence more strongly than a constant routine alone and is followed here, but the disagreement is genuine and this parameter should be treated as the weakest in the cardiovascular arm.

name: Time of peak mean arterial pressure
citation: Shea SA, Hilton MF, Hu K, Scheer FAJL. Existence of an endogenous circadian blood pressure rhythm in humans that peaks in the evening. Circ Res 2011;108(8):980-984.
notes: PRECISION: rounded to 3 significant figures on 2026-08-27. The sources do not support more, and carrying digits that do not exist forced the closure gate and the test suite to chase arithmetic noise. Derived rows inherit the significant figures of their inputs and are rounded to match; the closure tolerance was moved to 1e-3 in the same change, which is still an order of magnitude tighter than the 6% error that motivated that gate. || WAS 0.25 day (13:00) AND ASSUMED. Shea 2011 reports that all six peaks - systolic and diastolic across three protocols - occurred at a circadian phase corresponding to approximately 21:00, the biological evening. Under this component's convention that phase 0 is the start of the active period, taken as 07:00 for humans, 21:00 is 14 h later = 0.583333 day. DERIVED only in that clock time is converted to the component's phase convention. NOTE WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE MODEL: the ENDOGENOUS BP peak is in the EVENING, whereas the familiar ambulatory dip is NOCTURNAL. They are not the same rhythm and are not even in phase, which is the second reason the old dip-fraction parameterisation was wrong. Shea also reports the BP rhythm was unrelated in phase to those of cortisol, catecholamines, cardiac vagal modulation, heart rate or urine flow.

citation: Soares AA, Prates AB, Weinert LS, Veronese FV, de Azevedo MJ, Silveiro SP. Reference values for glomerular filtration rate in healthy Brazilian adults. notes: CHANGED 180.0 -> 152.6 L/day ON 2026-08-27. THE PREVIOUS VALUE WAS NOT SOURCED: the citation read 'Standard physiological reference. VERIFY.', which is not a reference, while extraction_method claimed `reported`. 180 L/day is 125 mL/min - the textbook figure - and MEASURED GFR in healthy adults is not 125. Pre-registered in validation/verify_rows_prereg.md, committed at e0195f4 before any source was opened. pooling_rule = single-source, k = 1. THE VALUE: 106 mL/min/1.73 m2 x 1440 / 1000 = 152.64 -> 152.6 L/day, 4 significant figures per directive 1.9. SD 18 mL/min/1.73 m2 -> 25.9 L/day. Under ADR 0014 this row therefore stays `both` with the cohort recorded, which is the rule's 'where only one value is supported, use it for both' branch and not a gap. N Engl J Med 2017;376(24):2349-2357. PMID 28614683. 1,388 healthy living kidney donors, iothalamate, mean GFR 115 +/- 24 mL/min ABSOLUTE and UNINDEXED. At a typical donor body surface area near 1.9 m2 that is about 105 mL/min/1.73 m2, agreeing closely with Soares - but the paper does not report the BSA needed to make that conversion, so it CANNOT be placed on this model's 1.73 m2 reference without an assumption. pooling.md prohibits pooling across incompatible measurement bases, and indexed against absolute is exactly that, so it is recorded as corroboration and NOT averaged in. Note also that Denic's cohort is screened kidney donors, i.e. selected for renal health above the population. WHY THE TEXTBOOK 125 IS HIGHER. The conventional figure predates routine clearance measurement in unselected healthy adults and is closer to a young-adult value; Soares finds 112 +/- 18 under 45 against 98 +/- 15 over 45, so an all-ages healthy mean sits well below 125. name: Fractional tubular sodium reabsorption at nominal pressure

This row is DERIVED and is not independent of GFR: a smaller filtered load needs a smaller reabsorbed fraction to excrete the same 205 mEq/day. Re-deriving it was mandatory, not optional - leaving it at 0.9918651 would have broken sodium balance by about 18%. The excreted fraction 1 - FR_Na moved 0.0081349 -> 0.0095956. The pre-registration fixed this dependency in advance precisely so the two could not be entered as though they were separate measurements. The arithmetic is exact: 1 - 205/(180*140) = 0.9918650793650794, matching the stored value to every digit it carries. Branch 1 of validation/verify_rows_prereg.md. NO NEW GATE WAS ADDED. tools/check_closure.py already asserts exactly this identity under 'Na excretion == Na intake' - directive 1.10, do not add what already exists. IT IS NOT INDEPENDENT OF RN.GFR.NOMINAL. If GFR moves this MUST move with it by the same derivation; re-entering them separately would break sodium balance silently. SIGNIFICANT FIGURES APPLY TO THE QUANTITY THAT CARRIES THE INFORMATION, WHICH HERE IS 1 - FR_Na, NOT FR_Na. This row was rounded to 4 significant figures (0.9919) on 2026-08-27 with everything else and immediately broke sodium balance: excretion 204.12 against intake 205, a 0.43% drift, because the excreted fraction is 0.0081 and four figures on FR_Na leaves only two on the difference. Restored to 0.9918651. A small difference of two large numbers needs enough digits on the large numbers to leave the difference meaningful - that is not false precision, it is the arithmetic. This is the same failure recorded in the header of tools/check_closure.py, where rounding this row to 0.9915 gave 214.2 against 205. || PRECISION: rounded to 4 significant figures on 2026-08-27. name: Pressure natriuresis slope
citation: Guyton AC, Coleman TG, Granger HJ. Circulation: overall regulation. Annu Rev Physiol 1972;34:13-46.
notes: CALIBRATED, not measured. VALUE UNCHANGED AT 20.0 - read the identifiability result below before altering it. Originating model: Guyton 1972 systems analysis; the EXISTENCE and steepness of pressure natriuresis is E1 and well replicated, this particular slope is a fitted constant that propagated through the modelling literature. FORM: LINEAR, AND NOW SOURCED. Roman RJ, Cowley AW Jr, Am J Physiol 1985, PMID 3970209 (rat, denervated, vasopressin/aldosterone/corticosterone/noradrenaline clamped) report the relation as the slope of a LINE, 2 uL/min/kidney/mmHg over RPP 90-160 mmHg. Osborn/Francisco/DiBona, Proc Soc Exp Biol Med 1981, independently report UNaV falling LINEARLY over dog RPP 137-55 mmHg. An earlier note in relations.csv called the curve 'markedly nonlinear'; that was asserted from memory and is RETRACTED. VALIDITY RANGE roughly 55-160 mmHg. RN.AUTOREG.UPPER was 180, outside that range; moved to 160 on 2026-08-21 and cited to the same paper. MAGNITUDE CROSS-CHECK: Mizelle HL et al, Hypertension 1993;22:102-110 (dog, split bladder, bilateral servo-control, 12 d - the cleanest isolation of pressure per se) gives 3.468 mmol/day/mmHg whole animal = 2.154e-4 of filtered load per mmHg against this row's 7.937e-4, so the calibrated value is 3.68x STEEPER than the animal datum on a scaling-free basis. That is the range in uncertainty_value; 5.43 is the Mizelle-consistent value. SINGLE SOURCE, k=1, DOG - per validation/pooling.md that is animal-derived, may not be pooled with a human value, and is recorded as a comparator rather than adopted. IDENTIFIABILITY (measured 2026-08-20 on IPE at 9a6fa42): this parameter ALONE fixes the model's salt sensitivity. At steady state excretion equals intake, so Na_excr = Na_filtered*(1-FR_Na) + G_pn*(MAP-MAP_ref) gives dMAP ~ d(intake)/G_pn, in which CV.VENOUS_RETURN.SENSITIVITY does not appear. Confirmed numerically: the 205->103 mEq/day step gives 4.934 mmHg at G_pn=20.0 and 15.698 mmHg at G_pn=5.43, while varying G_vr over 2880->600 at fixed G_pn=5.43 moves the shift only 15.698->12.403 and drives V_ecf to 9.889 L, below the 10 L floor asserted in test/runtests.jl. The residual departure from an exact 1/G_pn law is C_Na drift. CONSEQUENCE, correcting HANDOVER.md section 5 item 4: G_pn and G_vr are NOT jointly identified as one lumped loop gain. G_pn is identified by the salt-sensitivity shift and G_vr by ECF volume, separately. Adopting the Mizelle value in isolation re-balances nothing - it forces a 15.7 mmHg shift across a 102 mEq/day range, which is salt-sensitive-hypertensive behaviour, not normotensive. WHY THE GAP IS PROBABLY REAL RATHER THAN AN ERROR: IPE has NO volume-sensing natriuretic path. Seeliger et al, J Physiol 2004;559:939-951, servo-controlled RPP during saline loading in freely moving dogs with NO reduction in peak or cumulative natriuresis, and Bie 2018 (10.1152/ajpregu.00363.2017) argues excretion is keyed to extracellular volume rather than pressure. With ANP absent, all sodium regulation is forced through this one term, so an inflated G_pn is the expected COMPENSATION for the missing path. DO NOT lower this to 5.43 before a volume-sensing natriuretic path exists - doing so degrades the only behaviour the model has ever reproduced. Re-estimate G_pn and the ANP gain JOINTLY against digitised Mars500, as posteriors, not this value alone and not as a point value. || ADR 0013'S FALSIFIABLE TEST WAS RUN ON 2026-09-02 AND THE VALUE STAYS AT 20.0. Pre-registered in validation/ecf_salt_response_prereg.md; reproduce with python validation/ecf_salt_response_extract.py. ADR 0013 proposes 20.0 -> 51.0 on the human PRESSURE response and requires its volume test to pass BEFORE acceptance. It fails. van den Bosch 2021 (Physiol Rep 2021;9(24):e15103, PMID 34921521, n = 70 healthy men, 7 d per level, ECFV by iothalamate, intake verified by 24 h urinary sodium) gives dMAP/dV_ecf = 1.885 mmHg/L against the model's 9.80 at that cohort's 80.6 kg - a factor of 5.2 against a pre-registered failure threshold of 2, and it fails on all three volume proxies so it does not turn on the iothalamate space or the 1 kg = 1 L conversion. THE FAILURE IS NOT ABOUT THIS ROW. G_pn and CV.VENOUS_RETURN.SENSITIVITY are ORTHOGONAL, measured: an 8x change in G_vr moves the pressure response by 0.12% and moves the volume response exactly inversely. G_pn sets dMAP; G_vr sets dMAP/dV_ecf. So the human pressure data and the human volume data identify one parameter each with no cross-talk, and the pressure limb still supports 51. What the test shows is that ACCEPTING 51 ALONE WOULD MAKE THE VOLUME RESPONSE WORSE - from 1.26x too small at 20 to 3.2x too small at 51 - because dMAP is what this row moves and dV_ecf follows it down at a fixed, wrong ratio. Fix G_vr first, re-run the test, then accept. DECLARED CONFLICT: Heer 2000 (PMID 10751219) and Heer 2009 (PMID 19173770) report no total-body-water or body-mass increase on high sodium and a non-monotonic ECV response, which would put the error's sign the other way; that camp invokes osmotically inactive sodium storage, which is ADR 0004 and is default OFF here.

name: Lower limit of renal autoregulation
citation: Finke R, Gross R, Hackenthal E, Huber J, Kirchheim HR. Threshold pressure for the pressure-dependent renin release in the autoregulating kidney of conscious dogs. Pflugers Arch 1983;399(2):102-110. PMID 6139786. Lower limit of renal blood flow autoregulation, measured directly by servo-controlled stepwise reduction of renal artery pressure in the conscious animal.
notes: VALUE CHANGED 80.0 -> 63.9 mmHg ON 2026-08-27, AND SPECIES CORRECTED human -> dog. The previous value was NOT SOURCED: citation read 'Standard physiological reference. VERIFY.', which is not a reference, and species read 'human', which was not supported. This row was the last of the seven rows carrying that identical non-citation to be flagged as genuine debt rather than discharged, and HANDOVER 3.1 named it the one to look at first because CV.MAP.SETPOINT moved 93 -> 87 on the same day, carrying the operating point TOWARD this breakpoint. PRE-REGISTERED EXTRACTION: validation/autoreg_lower_prereg.md, committed at 3fbe260 BEFORE any paper was opened; executed by validation/autoreg_lower_extract.py. 26 PubMed queries in two sweeps, 1114 unique records screened. POOLING RULE, DECLARED BEFORE EXTRACTION per validation/pooling.md: single-source, n_studies k=1. No cross-species pooling was performed and no range midpoint was taken; both are prohibited for new entries. BRANCH 7 OF THE PRE-REGISTERED PROCEDURE WAS TAKEN. Branches 1-5 fail: NO human primary study reports a numeric lower breakpoint. The one that appears to - Textor SC et al, Ann Intern Med 1985;102(3):308-314, 'Critical perfusion pressure for renal function' - measures a STENOSIS threshold in bilateral atherosclerotic renovascular disease, not the intrinsic breakpoint of a normal kidney, and the sensitivity disappeared after revascularisation. Branch 6 fails too, and that is the finding of this pass: THE HUMAN EVIDENCE CONFLICTS AT THE SAME PRESSURE. At MAP 60 mmHg, Lessard MR and Trepanier CA, Anesthesiology 1991;74(5):860-865 (n=20, GFR by inulin, ERPF by PAH, MAP 59.8 +/- 0.4 for 237 min) found GFR not significantly further reduced and renal vascular resistance FALLING to maintain renal blood flow - the autoregulatory signature; while Hara T et al, J Clin Anesth 1998;10(7):539-545 (n=26, MAP 60 for 120 min) found creatinine clearance SIGNIFICANTLY DECREASED in both arms. Lessard is the methodologically stronger study, but choosing it after seeing both is precisely what pre-registration forbids, so branch 6's condition - that human studies ESTABLISH preservation - genuinely fails on its own terms. There is no lower pressure where the human evidence is unconflicted either: at MAP 50, Zayas VM et al, Am J Physiol 1993;265(5 Pt 2):F686-F692 and Toivonen J et al, Eur J Anaesthesiol 1991;8(1):13-20 both report renal function falling. ALL FOUR HUMAN STUDIES ARE ANAESTHESIA SAFETY STUDIES and directive 1.7 predicts what they returned: apply the test - had the physiology come out differently, the conclusion would have been 'this hypotensive technique is unsafe for the kidney'. The pressure-flow relationship is the INSTRUMENT there, not the subject, and every one of them carries a confound (volatile anaesthetic, sympathetic blockade, vasodilator, or all three), with anaesthesia depressing GFR before any pressure was lowered. THE ADOPTED SOURCE IS THE OPPOSITE KIND OF STUDY. Finke 1983 varied renal artery pressure from 160 to 40 mmHg in seven CONSCIOUS foxhounds under beta-blockade on a normal sodium diet (4.1 mmol/kg/day), reducing it in steps held constant by a servo-control system driving an inflatable renal artery cuff. Between 160 mmHg and resting pressure renal blood flow did not change; between resting pressure and the lower limit of autoregulation, average 63.9 mmHg, it rose only about 7%. The relationship IS the subject. No standard deviation is reported for the limit itself, so uncertainty_type stays none rather than inventing one - the paper does report 89.8 +/- 3.3 mmHg for its separate renin threshold, so the omission is the authors' and not a transcription loss. DECLARED CONFLICTS, LOGGED AND NOT RESOLVED. (1) Shipley RE, Study RS, Am J Physiol 1951;167(3):676-688, PMID 14903093 - the ANAESTHETISED dog study that is the origin of the textbook 80-180 and therefore of the value this row carried; its PubMed record carries the MeSH term 'Humans', a legacy-indexing artefact of the AJP back catalogue already flagged in autoreg_upper_prereg.md. Anaesthesia is the most likely single explanation of 80 vs 63.9. (2) Cupples WA, Braam B, Am J Physiol Renal Physiol 2007;292(4):F1105-F1123, PMID 17229679 - a tier B review putting the limit at ~75 mmHg in dog and ~85 in rat. pooling.md: the primary source wins and the divergence is logged. Averaging 75 and 85 would produce a number describing neither species. (3) The 2025 human review already cited in this row's previous note (doi 10.22514/sv.2025.001) holds that human evidence is insufficient for 80 as the lower limit; this extraction agrees and goes further - the human evidence that does exist puts the limit near 60. THE BRANCH CHOICE IS NOT LOAD-BEARING: branch 6 would have given 59.8 and branch 7 gives 63.9, a 4.1 mmHg difference, and no conclusion depends on which. Two independent lines - conscious dog with a measured breakpoint, anaesthetised humans bracketing 50 to 60 - different species, designs, decades and authors, both land near 60. NEITHER SUPPORTS 80. NO MODEL RESULT CHANGES. The three salt arms sit at MAP 81.900 / 84.450 / 87.001 mmHg, above the old 80 and above the new 63.9, so all remain on the autoregulation plateau and every steady state is bit-identical. The pre-registration declared this BEFORE extraction so that 'it does not change the answer' could not wave the change through, and so that a value above ~81.9 would have had to be escalated rather than quietly avoided. WHAT CHANGES IS MARGIN: the low-salt arm sat 1.9 mmHg above a piecewise kink and now sits 18.0 mmHg above it. STILL DEBT, AND THE REASON IS FIXED IN THE PRE-REGISTRATION. This is a dog number and the human experiment IS performable - humans have repeatedly been taken to 50-60 mmHg. The ethical-ceiling argument that earns RN.AUTOREG.UPPER its E2 standing under the ADR 0006 amendment does NOT transfer to this row, and was ruled out in the pre-registration before the search so it could not be reached for afterwards. What is missing is a study that lowers pressure in humans WITHOUT general anaesthesia and measures GFR by inulin at graded steps. Debt with a named primary source is a real improvement on a non-citation; it is not a closure. SEPARATELY, AND OUT OF SCOPE: Finke 1983 also measured the renin release threshold at 89.8 +/- 3.3 mmHg in conscious dog, against RAAS.RENIN.PRESSURE_THRESHOLD = 93.0 currently carried on van Ochten. NOT CHANGED HERE. Recorded because that row is the rectification point HANDOVER 3.1 found the model sitting exactly on, and a second independent primary source for it now exists in a paper this repo has read. THE PIECEWISE FORM REMAINS UNSOURCED: relations.csv row Renal.GFR keeps an empty form_citation and stays in GRANDFATHERED_UNSOURCED. A NUMBER was sourced, not an EQUATION. Finke in fact reports renal blood flow rising ~7% below resting pressure rather than staying flat, so the true plateau has a slight slope the model's ifelse does not represent.

name: Upper limit of renal autoregulation
citation: Roman RJ, Cowley AW Jr. Characterization of a new model for the study of pressure-natriuresis in the rat. Am J Physiol 1985;248:F190-F198. PMID 3970209. Highest renal perfusion pressure at which GFR was measured and found unchanged.
notes: EVIDENCE UNDER AN ETHICAL CEILING, NOT DEBT (ADR 0006 amended 2026-08-21). The rat provenance of this value is not a deficiency to be burned down. No human study raises arterial pressure to locate the failure of GFR autoregulation and none may; the human literature only ever lowers it. Where the human experiment cannot ethically exist, a well-conducted animal study is the evidence, not a substitute for it. This row is E2 with species, preparation and tested range recorded. WHAT REMAINS A REAL LIMITATION IS THE CENSORING, NOT THE SPECIES: 160 mmHg was the highest RPP tested in that preparation, so the true breakpoint is >= 160 and is not known to BE 160. UPPER BREAKPOINT MOVED 180 -> 160 mmHg ON 2026-08-21. The previous value was NOT SOURCED: citation read 'Standard physiological reference. VERIFY.' and species read 'human', neither of which was true. POOLING RULE, DECLARED BEFORE EXTRACTION per validation/pooling.md, pre-registration in validation/autoreg_upper_prereg.md: single-source, n_studies k=1. The pre-registration fixed, before any paper was read, that if zero HUMAN primary studies reported an upper breakpoint then the value could not be retained by cross-species pooling or by range-midpoint (both prohibited) and had to be brought inside the range where the model's own relations have support. SEARCH RESULT - THERE IS NO HUMAN PRIMARY EVIDENCE FOR AN UPPER BREAKPOINT. PubMed yields no human study that RAISES arterial pressure and measures the pressure at which GFR autoregulation fails; for obvious reasons the human literature only ever probes the LOWER limb by LOWERING pressure - Parving HH et al, Diabetologia 1984;27:547-552 (clonidine, MAP fall 16-18 mmHg, PMID 6442240), New JP et al, Diabetologia 1998;41:206-211 (trandolapril, MAP 103->93, PMID 9498655), Christensen PK et al, Kidney Int 2001 (PMID 11576357) and Diabetes Care 2003 (PMID 12502673). None of these reaches 160 mmHg, let alone 180. WHERE 180 ACTUALLY CAME FROM: Shipley RE, Study RS, Am J Physiol 1951;167:676-688, doi 10.1152/ajplegacy.1951.167.3.676, PMID 14903093 - DOG, acute alterations of renal artery pressure. That is the primary origin of the textbook '80-180 mmHg' and it is canine. (The PubMed MeSH record for PMID 14903093 carries the term 'Humans'; that is a known legacy-indexing artefact of the AJP back-catalogue, contradicted by the paper and by every secondary source that cites it as the canine range. Recorded here because the MeSH tag would otherwise look like human support.) 180 therefore entered this ledger as a dog number wearing a human label. WHAT IS ADOPTED: Roman RJ, Cowley AW Jr, Am J Physiol 1985;248:F190-F198, doi 10.1152/ajprenal.1985.248.2.F190, PMID 3970209. RAT, denervated kidney, vasopressin, aldosterone, corticosterone and noradrenaline clamped by infusion, RPP set by aortic clamp. Verbatim: 'Increasing RPP within the autoregulatory range from 90 to 160 mmHg produced 5- to 20-fold increases in urine flow and sodium excretion with no detectable changes in glomerular filtration rate, renal blood flow, or peritubular capillary pressure.' That is a direct primary measurement that GFR autoregulation is INTACT at 160 mmHg. THIS IS A CENSORED OBSERVATION, NOT A MEASURED BREAKPOINT. 160 mmHg is the highest RPP Roman and Cowley tested, so the true upper limit is >= 160; it is not known to BE 160. uncertainty_type is 'none' rather than a range because inventing a 160-180 interval would smuggle back the range-midpoint reasoning pooling.md prohibits. The model breakpoint is set at the edge of evidence, which is the conservative direction: it makes GFR fall with pressure slightly earlier than reality, rather than asserting a flat plateau in a region nothing has measured. WHY 160 AND NOT SOMETHING ELSE - THE TWO CONSTRAINTS COINCIDE. Roman and Cowley 1985 is ALSO the form source for the model's pressure natriuresis (see RN.PRESSURE_NATRIURESIS.SLOPE and ledger/relations.csv row Renal.FR_effective), where the LINEAR form is evidenced over roughly 55-160 mmHg. At 180 the autoregulation breakpoint sat OUTSIDE the range over which the equation it modifies has any support, so the model contained a kink in a region where its own natriuresis term was unevidenced. Setting the breakpoint to 160 makes the autoregulatory plateau and the natriuresis validity range terminate together, at the same pressure, from the SAME primary paper. That is not a coincidence chosen after the fact - the <=160 ceiling was written into the pre-registration before extraction. CROSS-SPECIES POOLING NOT PERFORMED, as prohibited. The dog value (Shipley 1951) and the rat value (Roman 1985) are NOT averaged. One rat study is adopted; the dog study is recorded as provenance archaeology for the discarded 180, not as a co-estimate. CORROBORATION, RECORDED AS CONTEXT AND NOT POOLED: Cupples WA, Braam B, Am J Physiol Renal Physiol 2007;292:F1105-F1123, doi 10.1152/ajprenal.00194.2006, describe the plateau as spanning from ~75 mmHg (dogs) or ~85 mmHg (rats) to >160 mmHg - note '>160', an open upper bound, not a fixed 180. Carlstrom M, Wilcox CS, Arendshorst WJ, Physiol Rev 2015;95:405-511, doi 10.1152/physrev.00042.2012, quote the conventional 80-180 mmHg. Both are reviews (tier B) and neither adds human primary data on the upper limit. SPECIES CHANGED human -> rat. TIER CHANGED B -> A: per SOURCES.md, tier A includes 'peer-reviewed primary research in animal models, flagged as such with species noted'. The tier RISES because the source is now a primary measurement rather than an unnamed reference, while the species flag FALLS to rat. Those are two separate axes and both moved honestly. KNOWN LIMITATION: the model is human. A rat autoregulatory breakpoint is being used in a human model because no human number exists. This is species extrapolation and is flagged as such. NO NUMERICAL EFFECT AT THE OPERATING POINT: IPE runs at MAP ~88-93 mmHg, inside [80, 160], where GFR ~ GFR0 either way. Verified: the ADR 0007 salt-step result is unchanged. The change buys honesty and removes an unevidenced kink, not different behaviour. WHAT IS STILL NOT SOURCED: the piecewise-flat-then-proportional FORM of the autoregulation equation, including its derivative discontinuity at both breakpoints. Only the breakpoint VALUE is sourced here. ledger/relations.csv row Renal.GFR therefore remains in the grandfathered unsourced list in tools/check_relations.py and its form_citation stays empty. LEDGER SCHEMA DEBT: validation/pooling.md specifies pooling_rule, n_studies and pooling_notes as columns of this CSV. Those columns do not exist yet, so the rule is recorded in prose here, following the precedent already set by RN.PRESSURE_NATRIURESIS.SLOPE. SCALING FROM RAT TO HUMAN: NO SCALING FACTOR IS APPLIED, AND THAT IS A DELIBERATE CLAIM, NOT AN OMISSION. This parameter is a PRESSURE (mmHg), an intensive variable, unlike the extensive quantities in this ledger (GFR, sodium excretion, blood volume) which would require allometric scaling by body or kidney mass. Mean arterial pressure in the conscious rat (~100-120 mmHg) and in the adult human (~93 mmHg here) are the same order of magnitude, and the autoregulatory plateau is generated by afferent-arteriolar myogenic tone and tubuloglomerular feedback, which are transmural-pressure-sensing mechanisms operating on the same pressure scale in both species rather than mass-dependent ones. Cupples and Braam 2007 report lower limits of ~75 mmHg (dog) and ~85 mmHg (rat) - a ~10 mmHg spread across a roughly 40-fold body-mass difference, which is the empirical evidence that this quantity does not scale with mass. The residual risk is therefore not a missing scale factor but genuine between-species difference in the breakpoint itself, of order 10 mmHg based on that spread, and it is unquantified in the upward direction because no species has been measured above 160 mmHg in this preparation. RE-FRAMED 2026-08-21 under the ADR 0006 amendment: an earlier version of this note treated 'not human' as a defect. It is not. What is genuinely unsourced here is the piecewise FORM of the autoregulation equation (see ledger/relations.csv row Renal.GFR) and the LOWER breakpoint - not this value's species.

name: Obligatory urine volume at maximal concentration
citation: Derived from RN.URINE.SOLUTE_LOAD and ADH.URINE.OSM_MAX.
notes: DERIVED 2026-09-01, AND THIS IS THE INVERSION THE ROW ITSELF ASKED FOR. V_min = RN.URINE.SOLUTE_LOAD / ADH.URINE.OSM_MAX = 600.0 / 982.0 = 0.611 L/day. Was 0.5, `assumed`, citation empty, from branch 6 of validation/verify_rows_prereg.md - whose note said the derivation in this ledger was probably inverted and that sourcing U_max and deriving this row was the right next move. It is now done, U_max is sourced from Tryding 1988, and the conventional 0.5 L/day was 18% low. THE MODEL HAD ALREADY INVERTED IT. Renal.jl records that V_min is deliberately no longer a parameter: since the urine solute load began tracking sodium excretion (2026-08-27) the floor is computed as Osm_load / U_max and varies with the salt arm. Nothing in src/ reads this row. tools/check_closure.py was its only consumer and was asserting the relationship in the OPPOSITE direction to the code it is supposed to be checking. That is fixed in the same change. TIER C, INHERITED FROM THE NUMERATOR AND NOT FROM THE DENOMINATOR. ADH.URINE.OSM_MAX is now tier A, but RN.URINE.SOLUTE_LOAD = 600 mOsm/day is an unsourced conventional figure that RN.URINE.SOLUTE_NONNA already records as too low for a Western diet - typical measured totals are 700-900. A larger true load would raise this floor proportionally. The weakest input sets the tier. WHAT IT MEANS PHYSICALLY: with a 600 mOsm/day load and a true maximal urine concentration of 982 mOsm/kg, urine output cannot fall below 611 mL/day. The old pairing claimed 500 mL, which required a concentrating ability nobody has measured.

name: Cardiac output at rest
citation: Derived from CV.HR.NOMINAL and CV.SV.NOMINAL.
notes: DERIVED 2026-09-01, AND THE DEPENDENCY IS NOW THE RIGHT WAY ROUND. CO0 = HR0 * SV0 * 1440 / 1000 = 62.0 * 96 * 1.44 = 8570.88 L/day (5.95 L/min). Exact - no rounding, because a derived row that closes an identity must carry every digit, the lesson CV.SV.NOMINAL recorded when it held that position. WHAT THIS ROW WAS. 7200 L/day, a `both` row, `assumed` with an EMPTY citation since branch 6 of validation/verify_rows_prereg.md, carrying the conventional 5 L/min x 1440. Its own note said the dependency was backwards and named this as the fix: stroke volume is what echocardiography and CMR MEASURE, cardiac output is what they compute. That is now done. name: Hematocrit
citation: Morales-Mendoza E, Suarez-Ramos MDP, Godoy-Corredor M, Gomez-Lopera N, Combariza-Vallejo JF, Murcia J, Isaza-Ruget MA. Reference intervals for hemoglobin and hematocrit adjusted for altitude, sex, and age: a big data-based study in the Colombian population. Med Sci (Basel) 2026;14(1):136. doi:10.3390/medsci14010136. PMID 41892851. 662,024 hematocrit results from apparently healthy adults, 2022-2024, stratified by sex, age and residential altitude; LOW-ALTITUDE stratum (<1100 m a.s.l.) taken.
notes: CHANGED 0.45 `both` -> 0.453 male / 0.395 female ON 2026-08-28. The previous value was NOT SOURCED: citation read 'Standard physiological reference. VERIFY.' while extraction_method claimed `reported`. Pre-registered in validation/verify_rows_prereg.md at e0195f4. pooling_rule = single-source, k = 1. THE INCUMBENT 0.45 WAS ESSENTIALLY THE MALE VALUE APPLIED TO EVERYONE. That is the specific shape of the error here, and it is why the prereg fixed in advance that this row was expected to be dimorphic: androgen-driven erythropoiesis is not a body-size effect and does not dissolve into body_mass. THE VALUE: median hematocrit in the LOW-ALTITUDE stratum, men 18-64 45.3% and women 18-50 39.5%. The low-altitude stratum is taken deliberately - hematocrit rises with residential altitude, and this model carries no altitude. In the same cohort the men's median climbs 45.3 -> 48.9% from <1100 m to 2000-3000 m, so choosing the stratum matters more than the choice between plausible sources. Medians rather than means because the paper reports medians. INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION, DELIBERATELY NOT POOLED: Fulgoni VL 3rd, Agarwal S, Kellogg MD, Lieberman HR. Establishing pediatric and adult RBC reference intervals with NHANES data using piecewise regression. Am J Clin Pathol 2019;151(2):128-142. PMID 30285066. NHANES 1999-2012, n = 44,328, nationally representative US healthy population. It reports REFERENCE INTERVALS, not central values: male 20-35 y 40.2-51.0%, female 20-45 y 32.5-45.2%. Both adopted medians sit comfortably inside those intervals. It is NOT pooled with the Colombian medians - an interval and a median are not the same statistic, the populations differ, and pooling.md prohibits range-midpoint for new entries, which is the only way an interval could have been turned into a point estimate here. FULGONI INDEPENDENTLY MAKES THE TEXTBOOK POINT: it reports that suggested hematocrit and haemoglobin reference values for older adult males are SUBSTANTIALLY LOWER than current standards - a male lower limit of 35.0% at 71-79 years against a non-age-based conventional 38.8%. THE MODEL IS CURRENTLY INSENSITIVE TO THIS ROW, AND THAT IS A STRUCTURAL FACT WORTH KNOWING RATHER THAN A REASON NOT TO SOURCE IT. Haematocrit enters only through V_blood = f_pv*V_ecf/(1-Hct), and CV.PLASMA.ECF_FRACTION is DERIVED as BV0*(1-Hct)/V_ecf, so f_pv/(1-Hct) = BV0/V_ecf identically and the haematocrit cancels. Verified empirically: entering this pair left every simulated result bit-identical. It will bite the moment f_pv is sourced independently - plasma volume as a fraction of extracellular volume is directly measurable - or when anything depending on viscosity or oxygen carriage exists. Until then this row is honest provenance for a quantity the model reports but does not yet use.

Parasympathetic activation is far faster (200-600 ms) but acts on heart rate, which is not a state in this cycle-averaged model (ADR 0002) - hence the lumped single-arm treatment. 3.0 s is the upper end of the stated range.

name: Baroreflex setpoint resetting time constant
citation: Dampney RAL. Resetting of the baroreflex control of sympathetic vasomotor activity during natural behaviors. Front Physiol 2017.
notes: ASSUMED. Baroreflex resetting is well established qualitatively - the reflex re-centres on prevailing pressure over hours to days, which is WHY it cannot set long-run arterial pressure. A specific human time constant is not reported in the sources consulted. 1 day is an order-of-magnitude placeholder. CRITICAL: this parameter is what makes the baroreflex a fast buffer rather than a long-term regulator. If it were infinite the reflex would set long-run pressure and the Guyton claim in ADR 0007 would be false. Sensitivity to it must be tested.

name: Maximum fractional change in TPR from baroreflex
citation: Saturation bound; see notes.
notes: ASSUMED. The baroreflex characteristic is sigmoidal and saturates; an unbounded linear gain would let TPR go negative under large pressure excursions. 0.5 means TPR can move at most +/-50 percent from baseline by reflex action alone. Placeholder chosen to keep the model well-posed under hemorrhage-scale perturbations, not extracted from a reported response range.

name: Renal perfusion pressure above which renin release plateaus
citation: van Ochten M, El Fathi W, Bovee EME, Spaanderman MEA, Hooijmans CR, van Drongelen J. The renal baroreflex: a systematic review and meta-analysis in healthy and hypertensive animals. Physiol Rep 2025;13(17):e70547.
notes: THE COINCIDENCE IS BROKEN AS OF 2026-08-27, AND IT WAS THE FRAGILITY THIS ROW WARNED ABOUT. This threshold, 93 mmHg from van Ochten, used to equal CV.MAP.SETPOINT exactly, so the model sat ON the rectification point and RAAS was inactive at baseline BY CONSTRUCTION. The note said that rested on one unverified number. It did: the setpoint was the textbook brachial 120/80 convention and is now 87.0, derived from sourced central pressure. The model therefore sits 6 mmHg BELOW threshold and RAAS IS NOW ACTIVE AT REST - renin drive 0.069, plasma renin activity 2.31x baseline. That is more physiological, not less: resting renin is not zero. || Meta-analysis of 30 animal studies: renin falls linearly with rising renal pressure and plateaus above 93 +/- 2 mmHg. ADR 0006 E2 - servo-controlling renal perfusion pressure is not performable in humans, the same ethical ceiling as RN.PRESSURE_NATRIURESIS.SLOPE. QUALITY CAVEAT FROM THE PAPER ITSELF: risk of bias was high in most studies. FRAGILITY, RECORDED: this threshold equals CV.MAP.SETPOINT = 93.0, whose own citation reads 'Standard physiological reference. VERIFY.' The model therefore sits exactly ON the rectification threshold and RAAS is inactive at and above baseline BY CONSTRUCTION. That coincidence is doing structural work and rests on one unverified number. Verified against PubMed record PMID 40930784 on 2026-08-25. SCALING: none applied, and none is needed. The quantity is a PRESSURE THRESHOLD in mmHg, and arterial pressure is not body-size scaled across the mammals in this meta-analysis the way a flow or a volume would be - the threshold is reported in the same units the model uses. What is assumed instead is that the threshold TRANSFERS to humans unchanged, which is a species assumption rather than a scaling one, and it is the assumption to attack if this component misbehaves. Note the meta-analysis itself found the threshold comparable between healthy and hypertensive animals while the slope differed, which is weak evidence that the threshold is the more transferable of the two.

name: Aldosterone response to renin activity, log-log slope
citation: Walker WG, Moore MA, Horvath JS, Whelton PK. Arterial and venous angiotensin II in normal subjects. Circ Res 1976;38(6):477-483.
notes: DERIVED: log(5)/log(20) = 0.5372, from a 5-fold aldosterone rise against a 20-fold PRA rise across sodium restriction plus furosemide versus sodium surfeit, 16 normal subjects. COMPRESSIVE - a power law with exponent below 1. THE EXPONENT IS AGAINST PRA, NOT ANGIOTENSIN II. The parked component docstring said 'aldosterone vs angiotensin'; Walker reports a 2.72-fold arterial AngII rise, so aldosterone against AngII is log-log 1.47 and EXPANSIVE. Attaching the PRA-derived exponent to an angiotensin variable would have been wrong, and the model state is named pra for that reason. Verified against PMID 773568 on 2026-08-25.

name: Time constant of escape from mineralocorticoid sodium retention
citation: Kelly TM, Nelson DH. Sodium excretion and atrial natriuretic peptide levels during mineralocorticoid administration. Endocr Res 1987;13(4):363-383.
notes: DERIVED from the reported time course, not read off directly. Urinary sodium fell 27% immediately on fludrocortisone and returned to baseline levels in an average of 5 days, in four healthy males at 180 +/- 2 mEq/day. Modelling that as first-order recovery reaching 95% at 5 days gives tau = 5/ln(20) = 1.669 day. THE 95% CONVENTION IS A CHOICE and is recorded as one; 5/3 is within 0.1% of it. n=4, single study, so this is the weakest link in the escape path. Attribution was corrected once already, from 'Yokota N et al.' on 2026-08-21; re-verified against PMID 2966064 on 2026-08-25 and authors and every quoted number check out.

WHAT IT CANNOT DO: because escape drives fr_mod to zero at steady state, this parameter shapes the TRANSIENT only and cannot move any steady-state salt-step pressure. It is therefore far less consequential than CV.VENOUS_RETURN.SENSITIVITY or the natriuresis slope. Source it before using this component for anything transient.

name: Osmotic threshold for vasopressin release
citation: Zerbe RL, Miller JZ, Robertson GL. The reproducibility and heritability of individual differences in osmoregulatory function in normal human subjects. J Lab Clin Med 1991;117(1):51-59.

Individual thresholds ranged 280 to 288 mOsm/kg and the frequency distribution across 80 healthy adults was essentially normal, so the MIDPOINT 284.0 is adopted and the range is carried as the uncertainty rather than an SD, which the paper does not give in a poolable form. Thresholds correlated within monozygotic but not dizygotic twins. NOTE the companion SENSITIVITY spans 0.12 to 1.66 pg/ml per mOsm/kg - fourteen-fold, and highly reproducible within a subject at r = 0.94 - which is NOT used here because this model carries no plasma vasopressin concentration. That spread is the obvious population covariate for src/ensemble.jl. Verified against PMID 1987308 on 2026-08-25.

name: Minimum urine osmolality at full water diuresis
notes: ASSUMED and NOT SOURCED. A relationship-shaped search for maximal and minimal urinary concentrating ability in healthy humans returned lithium cohorts, hydration indices and clinical case series - none characterising the limit in a healthy population in a form this model can consume. 50 mOsm/kg is the conventional figure and it is recorded as an assumption rather than dressed in a textbook citation nobody opened. IT SETS THE MAXIMAL DIURESIS: with the assumed solute load it gives 12.0 L/day, which is plausible but unverified. Source this before using the component near the dilute end.

name: Maximum urine osmolality at maximal antidiuresis
citation: Tryding N, Berg B, Ekman S, Nilsson JE, Sterner G, Harris A. DDAVP test for renal concentration capacity. Age-related reference intervals. Scand J Urol Nephrol 1988;22(2):141-145.
notes: SOURCED 2026-09-01, AND THE TEXTBOOK 1200 WAS HIGH. Was 1200.0 mOsm/kg, DERIVED as RN.URINE.SOLUTE_LOAD / RN.H2O.OBLIGATORY_LOSS = 600 / 0.5 - maximal concentrating ability computed from an obligatory volume that was itself `assumed` with an empty citation. The dependency was backwards: MAXIMAL CONCENTRATING ABILITY IS WHAT IS MEASURED, by water deprivation or DDAVP, and the obligatory volume is what follows from it given a solute load. RN.H2O.OBLIGATORY_LOSS is now derived from this row. Pre-re-registered in validation/dependency_inversion_prereg.md, which was committed BEFORE any paper was opened and sits immediately before this change in main's history. NO COMMIT SHA IS CITED, DELIBERATELY - rebase-merge rewrites it and every such citation already in this ledger points at a commit main does not contain. Verify the ordering instead: git log --diff-filter=A -- validation/dependency_inversion_prereg.md. NOW REPORTED: Tryding 1988. Maximal urinary concentration after a single 4 microgram subcutaneous injection of DDAVP in 212 healthy adults aged 20 to 80. Mean values decline significantly with age, 982 mOsm/kg at 20 years to 823 at 80. 982 IS THE VALUE AT THE YOUNG ADULT END and is adopted because U_max is a CEILING - the saturation limit of the ADH curve in Adh.jl, reached at adh = 1 - rather than a population mean. The age decline is real, is roughly 16% across six decades, and this model has no age dimension: recorded as debt, not approximated. The same paper reports that maximal osmolality did not differ significantly between strict fluid restriction and liberal intake before the DDAVP, so the number is not an artefact of the deprivation protocol. CORROBORATED, NOT POOLED. Bech AP, Wetzels JFM, Nijenhuis T. Reference values of renal tubular function tests are dependent on age and kidney function. Physiol Rep 2017;5(23):e13542. Median maximal urine osmolality after desmopressin 1002 mOsm/kg in healthy individuals aged 18-50, 820 in healthy individuals over 50, 624 with compromised renal function. Two independent studies thirty years apart, both near 1000 in young healthy adults and both near 820 in the old. NOT POOLED: Bech reports a MEDIAN of 10 subjects and Tryding a fitted mean by age, and pooling.md forbids inventing a rule that fits them. SINGLE SOURCE, k = 1, rule 6. WHAT WAS SCREENED AND NOT USED. Fourteen further queries over two sweeps returned paediatric series, lithium and polycystic-kidney cohorts, desmopressin bioequivalence studies and hydration-marker papers. Nadvornikova 1980 (Clin Nephrol 1980;14(3):142-147, 45 healthy volunteers, standardised DDAVP protocol) is the right design but reports no normative osmolality in the record read. Curtis 1979 (Br Med J 1979;1(6159):304-305) reports that most normal subjects reach maximal concentration spontaneously over 24 hours, which supports the protocol but gives no value. NO DISPERSION IS ENTERED. Tryding reports age-related reference INTERVALS; the record read gives the age-related means, not an SD at a given age. Directive 1.12 wants a centre with spread and this row has only the centre - recorded rather than invented.

name: Normalised antidiuretic activity per mOsm/kg above threshold
citation: Derived to close baseline water balance; see notes.
notes: PRECISION: rounded to 3 significant figures on 2026-08-27. The sources do not support more, and carrying digits that do not exist forced the closure gate and the test suite to chase arithmetic noise. Derived rows inherit the significant figures of their inputs and are rounded to match; the closure tolerance was moved to 1e-3 in the same change, which is still an order of magnitude tighter than the 6% error that motivated that gate. || DERIVED, not fitted and not assumed. Forced by requiring that at the plasma osmolality setpoint the model excretes exactly intake minus insensible loss, which is what the pre-ADH placeholder did. k_adh = ((solute/(intake-insensible)) - U_min) / ((U_max - U_min) * (Osm_set - Osm_thr)) = 0.08780904 per mOsm/kg, giving antidiuretic activity 0.263427 at baseline - a quarter of maximal, with room to move both ways. Closure constraint enforced by tools/check_closure.py. THIS IS NOT ZERBE'S SENSITIVITY: that is 0.12-1.66 pg/ml per mOsm/kg and this is a normalised 0-1 activity, because no sourced map from plasma vasopressin to urine osmolality was found. || RECOMPUTED 2026-09-01, 0.0878 -> 0.10835, when ADH.URINE.OSM_MAX moved 1200 -> 982 (Tryding 1988). k_adh = ((solute/v_base) - U_min) / ((U_max - U_min) * (Osm_set - Osm_thr)) = (352.941176 - 50) / (932 * 3). The DERIVATION is unchanged and so is the operating point it pins: at the plasma osmolality setpoint the model still excretes exactly intake minus insensible loss, by construction. What changes is the SLOPE - a lower ceiling reached over the same osmolality span means each mOsm/kg buys more antidiuretic activity. Five significant figures because the closure check compares this against its own derivation at 1e-3 relative and three figures would fail it.

name: Daily urinary solute excretion
notes: ASSUMED and NOT SOURCED, and it is the load-bearing assumption of the ADH component - urine volume is this divided by urine osmolality, so it scales the whole water-excretion limb. 600 mOsm/day is a conventional adult figure. It is HELD CONSTANT, which is itself a modelling choice: in reality it tracks protein and salt intake, so a salt step should move it and here it does not. That omission makes the model under-respond to a salt load on the water side. Source it, and consider making it depend on Na_excr, before trusting any water result under a changed diet.

name: Urinary osmoles per mEq of sodium excreted
citation: Imamura T, Kinugawa K, Minatsuki S, Muraoka H, Kato N, Inaba T, Maki H, Shiga T, Hatano M, Yao A, Kyo S, Komuro I. Urine osmolality estimated using urine urea nitrogen, sodium and creatinine can effectively predict response to tolvaptan in decompensated heart failure patients. Circ J 2013;77(5):1208-1213. PMID 23318562. The validated estimator carries urine sodium with a coefficient of 2.
notes: THE COEFFICIENT IS ELECTRONEUTRALITY, NOT A FITTED CONSTANT. Every sodium ion leaving in the urine leaves with an accompanying anion, predominantly chloride, so one mEq of excreted sodium contributes approximately two milliosmoles - one for the cation and one for the anion. That is why the standard urine osmolality estimators all carry urine sodium with a coefficient of 2. WHAT THE CITATION ACTUALLY SUPPLIES. Imamura 2013 validated the whole estimator 1.07*(2*[urine Na] + [urine urea nitrogen]/2.8 + [urine creatinine]*2/3) + 16 against MEASURED urine osmolality in 66 patients and reports r = 0.938, p < 0.001. The paper does not measure this coefficient; it measures that a formula containing it reproduces the real thing. That is the honest description of the evidence and is why this row is tier B rather than A. DECLARED LIMITATION OF THE COHORT: decompensated heart failure patients receiving tolvaptan, i.e. a diseased population under a V2 antagonist. Directive 1.7 test - had the correlation come out poorly, the conclusion would have been that estimated urine osmolality cannot predict tolvaptan response, so the composition relation is the INSTRUMENT there and not the subject. It is accepted anyway because the coefficient is not an empirical finding of that paper but a charge-balance requirement, and the validation is corroboration that the requirement holds in real urine. INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION OF THE STRUCTURE, not pooled with it: Alwis US, Delanghe J, Dossche L, Walle JV, Van Camp J, Monaghan TF, Roggeman S, Everaert K. Could evening dietary protein intake play a role in nocturnal polyuria? J Clin Med 2020;9(8):2532. PMID 32764521. 170 subjects, 24 h collections in 8 timed samples with volume, osmolality, creatinine, urea and sodium all measured; reports urea as the largest single contributor to urine osmolality with sodium excretion the other major term. That is the two-part structure this row and RN.URINE.SOLUTE_NONNA implement.

name: Non-sodium urinary solute load, held constant
citation: Derived from RN.URINE.SOLUTE_LOAD, RN.URINE.OSM_PER_NA and BF.NA.INTAKE_MID.
notes: DERIVED, and it is a RESIDUAL rather than a measurement: SOLUTE_NONNA = RN.URINE.SOLUTE_LOAD - RN.URINE.OSM_PER_NA * BF.NA.INTAKE_MID = 600.0 - 2.0 * 154.0 = 292.0 mOsm/day. It stands for urea plus potassium salts plus everything else, all held constant. WHY IT IS DEFINED THIS WAY. RN.URINE.SOLUTE_LOAD is load-bearing: ADH.URINE.OSM_MAX, ADH.URINE.OSM_BASELINE and ADH.OSM.SENSITIVITY are all derived from it and four closure checks depend on it. Making the solute load track sodium must therefore leave the REFERENCE load untouched, or every derived ADH constant and every steady state moves. Pinning the residual so that total load returns exactly 600.0 at the mid salt arm (154 mEq/day) achieves that: the mid arm is unchanged to the last digit and only the high and low arms move. INHERITED DEBT, STATED PLAINLY: 292 mOsm/day is almost certainly TOO LOW for the non-sodium fraction. Urea alone is normally the largest single contributor to urine osmolality (Alwis 2020) and potassium salts add roughly another 100-120 mOsm/day, so a real non-sodium remainder on a Western diet is nearer 400-500. The residual is small because the parent RN.URINE.SOLUTE_LOAD = 600 mOsm/day is itself an unsourced conventional figure that is low for a 154 mEq/day sodium intake - typical measured totals are 700-900. THIS ROW DOES NOT FIX THAT AND MUST NOT BE READ AS FIXING IT. Correcting the total would move U_max, U_base, k_adh and every steady state, and needs its own pre-registered extraction. What this row does is make the load RESPOND to salt, which it previously did not do at all. Tier C, inherited from the parent.

name: Marker: the urinary sodium rhythm persists under constant routine
citation: el-Hajj Fuleihan G, Klerman EB, Brown EN, Choe Y, Brown EM, Czeisler CA. The parathyroid hormone circadian rhythm is truly endogenous - a general clinical research center study. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 1997;82(1):281-286.
notes: STRUCTURE MARKER, contributes no numeric value to any equation - it records WHY the renal arm is modelled as an endogenous driver at all, which is the claim ADR 0005 rests on. el-Hajj Fuleihan 1997: 11 healthy male volunteers, 36 h baseline followed by 28-40 h of constant routine - enforced wakefulness, strict semirecumbent posture, hourly snacks. Urinary calcium/creatinine, phosphate/creatinine and sodium/creatinine all showed a diurnal rhythm at baseline; the calcium and phosphate rhythms changed character under constant routine WHEREAS THAT OF URINARY SODIUM/CREATININE WAS UNCHANGED. An unmasked rhythm that survives removal of sleep, posture and meal timing is endogenous. CONTRAST WITH THE CARDIOVASCULAR ARM, where the same class of experiment is in open disagreement - see CIRC.CV_MAP.AMPLITUDE. The renal arm's premise is on firmer ground than the cardiovascular arm's, which is the reverse of what the placeholder parameters implied.

name: Resting heart rate, supine
citation: Gonzales TI, Jeon JY, Lindsay T, Westgate K, Perez-Pozuelo I, Hollidge S, Wijndaele K, Rennie K, Forouhi N, Griffin S, Wareham N, Brage S. Resting heart rate is a population-level biomarker of cardiorespiratory fitness: the Fenland Study. PLoS One 2023;18(5):e0285272.
notes: PRECISION: rounded to 2 significant figures on 2026-08-27. The sources do not support more, and carrying digits that do not exist forced the closure gate and the test suite to chase arithmetic noise. Derived rows inherit the significant figures of their inputs and are rounded to match; the closure tolerance was moved to 1e-3 in the same change, which is still an order of magnitude tighter than the 6% error that motivated that gate. || SUPINE resting heart rate. The Fenland Study reports a POOLED supine mean of 63.5 +/- 8.9 bpm across 10865 adults aged 29-65 (5722 women, 5143 men), and separately that 'on average, RHR was 3 bpm higher in women compared to men'. Solving those two statements with the exact group sizes gives male 61.9201 and female 64.9201. DERIVED, not read off: the paper does not tabulate sex-stratified supine means in the text, so this is arithmetic on two reported quantities. CAVEAT, RECORDED: the 3 bpm sentence says 'RHR' without naming a posture, and the paper reports three (seated 67.6, supine 63.5, sleeping 56.9). It is applied to supine here because supine is the posture this model uses, but if the difference is in fact a seated or pooled-across-posture figure the split is misattributed. The POOLED value is solid; the SPLIT carries this caveat. SUPINE IS THE POSTURE THE MODEL NEEDS: CV.CO.NOMINAL is itself derived from the conventional resting 5 L/min, which is a supine figure. Measured by chest sensor after at least 1 h rest, value taken from the final 3 min of a 6 min recording - a better-defined resting condition than a clinic pulse. COHORT: general population recruited from GP lists in Cambridgeshire, NOT health-screened. Uncertainty carries the POOLED SD; the paper gives no sex-stratified SD. CORROBORATION SEARCHED FOR AND NOT FOUND, recorded so it is not re-searched: three query families over resting heart rate by sex - reference/normal values, sex-differences, and population cohorts - returned risk-association studies (RHR as a predictor of stroke, cancer mortality, atrial fibrillation) rather than reference-value studies reporting sex-stratified resting means. This is a SINGLE-SOURCE pair and pooling.md rule 6 applies: say so, do not dress it as consensus. It is still better than the shared male-nominal value it replaces, because the pairing rule makes the female case explicit rather than implicit.

Cohort: 804 participants remaining after exclusion for non-Caucasian ethnicity, known cardiovascular disease and any condition affecting chamber size or function, of whom 800 (368 men, 432 women) have ventricular measurements. NOT NORMALISED TO THE REFERENCE MASS, AND THAT IS RECORDED DEBT RATHER THAN A CHOICE. This value is EXTENSIVE and is multiplied by size_factor = body_mass / BF.BODY_MASS.REFERENCE, so it should be stated at 70 kg. Petersen reports body weight by AGE GROUP (71, 71, 69 kg) but NOT by sex, so the cohort mean is essentially the reference mass while the male and female subgroups plainly are not. The pre-registration fixed the rule in advance: normalise where cohort mass is reported by sex, otherwise enter as reported and record the mismatch. So this pair still carries a body-size component, and in the ensemble - where mass is sampled by sex - that component is counted twice. Fixing it needs sex-stratified cohort mass or a BSA row. AND THE PREDICTION FIXED IN ADVANCE WAS HALF WRONG, WHICH IS THE USEFUL PART. The previous note on this row cited Katori 1979 for NO significant sex difference in stroke INDEX and concluded the dimorphism is body size, not the heart. Petersen indexes to BSA and the difference SURVIVES: 49 +/- 10 male against 45 +/- 8 female mL/m2, a 9% male excess where the absolute difference is 28%. Luu 2022 finds the same on 3206 people (46 vs 42), Salton 2002 states volumetric measures remain greater in men after BSA adjustment, and Le Ven 2016 states all gender differences remained after normalisation. Four independent cohorts. So body size carries roughly two thirds of the difference and about a third is not size - the pair was expected to collapse the way ECF per kg did when blood volume and haematocrit were sourced, and it does not.

name: Central pulse pressure, nominal
citation: Derived from CV.SBP.CENTRAL_NOMINAL and CV.DBP.CENTRAL_NOMINAL.
notes: DERIVED: PP = SBP - DBP = 109 - 76 = 33 mmHg, which reproduces the central pulse pressure of 33 mmHg the paper reports independently. That agreement is a check on the extraction, not a coincidence. Closure constraint.

name: Fraction of pulse pressure lying BELOW mean pressure
notes: ASSUMED at the conventional one third, which is the familiar MAP = DBP + PP/3. Discharges the TODO in reconstruct.jl, which carried this as a HARDCODED default of 0.4 and demanded a ledger row before the function was used for anything - directive 1.4 is now satisfied. NAME AND JUSTIFICATION CORRECTED 2026-08-27; THE VALUE IS UNCHANGED AND WAS ALWAYS RIGHT. This row was entered as 'Fraction of pulse pressure lying ABOVE mean pressure', and 0.3333 is the fraction lying BELOW it. Against the tier A central pressures in this same ledger - SBP 109, DBP 76, PP 33, MAP 87 - the fraction above the mean is (109-87)/33 = 0.667 and the fraction below is (87-76)/33 = 0.333. The old note's reasoning was inverted in the same way: it said 'the fraction of pulse pressure above mean must be below 0.5 because diastole is longer than systole', and diastole being longer is exactly why MAP sits NEARER DIASTOLIC, which makes the fraction BELOW the mean the one that must be under 0.5. The 0.515 that exposed the brachial/central mixing was (93-76)/33, a below-mean fraction, so the impossibility argument itself was correct and only its label was wrong. WHY IT MATTERED. check_closure.py uses this row as MAP = DBP + k*PP, i.e. with the CORRECT below-mean meaning, and passes. reconstruct.jl defined its form_factor as the fraction ABOVE the mean and computed SBP = MAP + form_factor*PP. Wiring the ledger row into that function under the shared name 'form factor' would have produced SBP 98.0 and DBP 65.0 against the sourced 109 and 76 - both wrong by PP/3 = 11 mmHg, in opposite directions - and NO GATE WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT, because the closure check never reaches reconstruct.jl. Found while connecting that file, not by any check. reconstruct.jl now takes k_below explicitly and names the convention in its signature. NOT CONSTANT IN REALITY, and reconstruct.jl calls treating it as constant the single largest error source in the reconstruction: it varies with heart rate, arterial stiffness, disease state, and - as the 87 versus 89.8 discrepancy shows - with measurement site. Source it before any claim about pulse pressure as an endpoint.

name: Total arterial compliance
citation: Derived from CV.SV.NOMINAL and CV.PP.CENTRAL_NOMINAL; form validated by Chemla 1998.
notes: RECOMPUTED 2026-09-01 when CV.SV.NOMINAL was sourced. C_art = SV0 / PP0 = 96 / 33.0 = 2.909 mL/mmHg. Was 2.445. DERIVED, and this is why agreement with the sourced 109/76 is CONSISTENCY AND NOT VALIDATION: the compliance is defined so that the reconstruction returns the sourced pulse pressure at the nominal stroke volume. It cannot disagree at the operating point. What it can do is get the RESPONSE wrong, and that is what moves now - a larger stroke volume with a proportionally larger compliance leaves nominal PP identical while changing how PP responds to a volume excursion. The Chemla 1998 SV/PP estimator is defined on AORTIC pressure, which is why PP here is the central value. See CV.MAP.SETPOINT for what happened the last time a brachial number was mixed with a central one.
